title: ME04a: When the System Becomes the Weather
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Through the fictional leader Maya, Claydon dramatises the gap between understanding an organisational system and acting inside it. Watching a sound strategy proposal die in a senior meeting, Maya reads the scene through five lenses: machine, living system, cultural ritual, power terrain and psychic fear. The breakthrough is not the analysis but the realisation that, despite all her theory, she did nothing to shift the room. The essay argues that leaders need attunement, a felt sense of when to act, adapt or hold still, not just more frames. It closes by distinguishing reflection-on-action, the studio replay, from reflection-in-action, the storm, and offers prompts on self, role and system for practising both.
points: A proposal can fail because of how a system protects itself, not because the idea is weak, and the five-lens reading makes that visible.
Insight alone is insufficient: Maya sees everything yet intervenes in nothing, which is the essay's central indictment of detached analysis.
The leader's task shifts from asking why something did not land to asking what kind of terrain the group is in.
Attunement, sensing when a lens is active and when to move or stay still, is offered as the missing leadership capacity.
Leadership in complexity needs both reflection-on-action and reflection-in-action, the studio's perspective and the storm's posture.
quotes: It was a smart proposal. The strategy lead had laid it out clearly: tighter priorities, cross-functional stretch, cleaner alignment. There was logic.
It wasn’t just a bad meeting. It was a full-body expression of system logic. A choreography of protection and persistence.
The room wasn’t disinterested. It was frightened. Nobody named it, but Maya could feel it.
But that wasn’t the breakthrough. The breakthrough was this: Even with all that awareness, she hadn’t done anything.
She didn’t want more clarity. She wanted traction. She didn’t want to describe the system. She wanted to intervene without breaking herself.
In that moment, she stopped asking, “Why didn’t that land?” And started asking, “What kind of terrain are we in?
Leadership in complexity, she realised, would require both: The studio’s perspective. And the storm’s posture.
